topic: organising a village chess league season

provenance.author: glowny-en-f
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is fixture and calendar arithmetic for the same league with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of a season that overruns. Grounded external referent: the fixture board in the hall, introduced in turn 0 and carried through the whole diagnosis (it holds the round cards, its side rail collects postponements, and it is mentioned directly before every insertion).

a: Here are the eight teams for the coming season, and their fixtures need counting before the cards are printed.
A single round robin gives every team seven matches, one match against each of the other sides.
Each match uses four boards, and each board produces one game between the two named players.
Count the matches in the full season first, and then count the games across all of those matches.
How many games does a single round robin of eight teams come to in total?
base: Our village chess league keeps sliding past Easter, and the last round is played to half empty tables.
Eight teams meet in the hall on Tuesdays, and every pairing hangs on the fixture board by the door.
The board holds seven rows of cards, one row for each round, and postponed matches crowd its side rail.
By March the rail carries more cards than the rows do, and nobody can say which games still count.
Where would you start trimming a season that keeps growing at the far end like this?

a: A single round robin of eight teams needs seven rounds, with four matches played in every one of them.
Seven rounds of four matches come to twenty-eight matches across the whole season when they are taken together.
Each match holds four games, so the season produces one hundred twelve games in total.
Printing needs one card per match, plus one spare card per round in case of corrections.
Does the print run of thirty-five cards cover all rounds with their spares included?
base: I would start with the rail, because a season is only as long as its slowest postponements.
Seven rounds should take seven Tuesdays, yet your board is plainly carrying half a season of spare games.
A postponed match with no fixed date is not a fixture, it is a promise nobody keeps.
I would give every card on the board a printed date before the season even opens.
Do the teams agree their postponement dates themselves, or does anyone hold them to a deadline?

a: Now work out the season calendar, counting club Tuesdays from week one at the start of October.
Rounds fill consecutive open weeks, and weeks three, five and six are blocked with no play.
A blocked week is skipped completely, and the next round simply waits for the next open week.
Lay the seven rounds onto the open weeks in order and name the closing week.
Which week number ends the season once those three blocked weeks are skipped in the count?
base: Nobody holds anyone to a deadline, and the captains sort dates out between themselves when they remember.
The board has hung in the hall for twenty years and its rows have never once changed.
Our hall is shared with the badminton club, so a lost Tuesday cannot simply move to Wednesday.
Two winter Tuesdays usually go to weather, and one more goes to the hall's own quiz night.
Would printed deadlines really survive their first collision with a flooded road in January?

a: Round one takes week one and round two takes week two, before the first block.
Week three is blocked, so round three lands on week four in the open sequence.
Weeks five and six are blocked, which pushes round four out to week seven.
Rounds five, six and seven then fill weeks eight, nine and ten without further gaps.
Which week closes the season under the plain count with no blocked weeks at all?
base: Deadlines survive January when the fixture, not the postponement, is the thing that moves.
Build two spare Tuesdays into the calendar from the start, one in December and one in February.
A washed out round then slides whole into the next spare slot instead of scattering into promises.
The rail on your board should hold nothing but the current round's unfinished cards.
Could your captains accept a rule that a game unplayed by the spare slot is simply drawn?

a: One correction before the cards are printed: the league has nine teams, not eight, this season.
A nine team round robin needs nine rounds, and one team sits out each round.
Recalculate the matches in the full season and the games, still keeping four boards per match.
Then say how many open weeks the longer season needs under the same three blocked weeks.
How many matches does each single round now hold with one team standing idle?
base: A drawn game rule would cause a riot at the top, but the middle tables might welcome it.
Our strongest two teams treat every half point as treasure and argue every date to the last.
The board does quietly settle some of this, because a card left on the rail embarrasses its captain.
Shame moves faster than any rule we have ever written down for the league.
Should the spare slots be published with the calendar, or held back like a referee's card?

a: Nine teams give thirty-six matches in a single round robin across the whole season.
Each round holds four matches while the ninth team stands idle for that week.
Four boards per match keep the count at one hundred forty-four games for the season.
Nine rounds need nine open weeks, so the season now closes in week twelve.
Does a print run of forty-five cards cover the thirty-six matches plus one spare per round?
base: Publish the spare slots, because a hidden safety net changes nobody's behaviour until it is too late.
The top teams will still argue, but they will argue inside a frame everyone can see.
Let the board carry the two spare weeks as empty rows of their own.
An empty row that fills up in January tells the whole club the season is still healthy.
Would the captains meet once in November to review the rail before winter sets in?

a: Now split the forty-five printed cards between the two record folders for the season.
Folder one takes the cards for rounds one to five, and folder two takes the rest.
Every round contributes four match cards and one spare card to its own folder.
Count the cards in each folder and check the two counts against the print run.
How many cards sit in folder two when rounds six to nine are filed there?
base: A November meeting could work, since the captains already gather for the county cup draw then.
We could walk them past the board and read the rail aloud, card by card.
Anything still unplayed gets a date that night or goes straight into the December spare slot.
The quiz night team will grumble about losing their Tuesday, but they grumble about everything.
Is one spare slot before Christmas actually enough for the weather we usually get?

a: Folder one holds rounds one to five, which is five rounds of five cards each.
That makes twenty-five cards in folder one when the spares are filed with their rounds.
Folder two holds rounds six to nine, which is four rounds of five cards each.
That makes twenty cards in folder two, and the folders together hold forty-five cards.
The two counts match the print run exactly, with no card left over.
base: One slot before Christmas is thin, and your own weather record argues for a second.
Two winter Tuesdays lost in a normal year means the December slot is spent before January starts.
Move the February slot earlier, or beg the badminton club for one Wednesday as a reserve.
A season that ends on time buys you goodwill for every rule you tighten next year.
Settle the reserve night before the season opens, not after the first flood.

a: Last job for tonight: give me the running card total folder by folder for checking.
Start from zero, add folder one, then add folder two, and state each running figure.
After that, list the rounds each folder covers in a single line for the noticeboard.
Keep the line short enough to fit the strip of card above the results table.
State the final figure again at the end so the checker sees it twice.
base: Wednesday is a real possibility, because the badminton club owes us for storing their nets all summer.
I will ask their secretary for the first Wednesday of December and of February.
The calendar then carries nine rounds, two spare Tuesdays and two reserve Wednesdays in plain view.
That feels like a season with walls instead of a season with wishes.
I will draft the whole thing this weekend and bring it to the committee.

a: The running total starts at zero and rises to twenty-five after folder one is added.
Adding folder two lifts the running total from twenty-five to forty-five at the close.
The noticeboard line reads folder one rounds one to five, folder two rounds six to nine.
That line fits the strip of card with room to spare at either end.
The final figure is forty-five cards, stated once more for the checker as asked.
base: Bring the draft as one sheet, with the rounds down the side and the dates across the top.
Committees approve what they can read in a minute and question everything that needs ten.
Ask for the drawn game rule last, once the calendar itself has already been nodded through.
If they balk, settle for the November review and try the rule again next season.
A league that finishes by Easter will make next year's argument for you.
